arithmetic.finding: The table's own arithmetic closes: input 4-16 ms + tick 1-3 ms + 2 vsyncs (33.3 ms) = 38-52 ms, matching 40/50 and 45/55. But the component model is a floor, not a typical: it omits the digitizer sample wait (0-8 ms at 120 Hz; WALT measured 22 ms physical contact to ACTION_DOWN on a 2016 Nexus 9, which gap-4 itself cites), the scan-out position (uniform 0-16.7 ms, mean 8.3) and panel response (2-8 ms), and on Android/iPad it applies the same 33 ms present as desktop even though the corpus's own native tables add a SurfaceFlinger/CA latch (+1 interval) that Chrome Android and WebKit also traverse. A Monte-Carlo of the explicit 60 Hz pipeline gives p50/p95 48/61 ms without and 65/78 ms with the OS-compositor latch, i.e. the web warm rows are about one 60 Hz frame optimistic at p50 and 1-1.5 frames at p95 on phones/iPad, exactly the perf judge's complaint re-emerging one frame later. With 1/2/3 present vsyncs the row would read 21-33 / 37-49 / 54-66 ms (W-4G input term). Because the gate is relative (REF + 1 frame) it is unaffected; what shifts is the absolute '≈45 → ≈25 ms' narrative, which from first principles is more like ≈55-65 → ≈20-25 ms (the native gain grows, it does not shrink). The 2-vsync floor remains unverified and Stage 0 G11 is the only settlement.

empirical.finding: The 2-vsync present floor itself cannot be measured here (headless has no display: Chromium's SwapStartToPresentation stage was 8 ms of SwiftShader software swap, not a vsync wait), so that term stays [unverified; Stage 0]. What Chromium's own EventLatency instrumentation does show is that the plan's input->tick term of 4-16 ms is wrong for wheel input: with a non-passive wheel handler Chromium delivers the event rAF-aligned to the next BeginMainFrame, RendererCompositorToMain alone is 16.0 ms p50 (one full 16.67 ms BeginFrame interval), and generation->end-of-main-thread-handling is 25-27 ms p50 / 31 ms p95 for CDP-injected events that carry no OS or USB hop; pointer events with a pending rAF (the viewer's tick model) measured 4.5 ms p50 / 14.4 ms p95, inside the plan's range, and pointer events with no pending rAF 1.1 ms. Generation->software-display for wheel was 33-38 ms p50 / 38-46 ms p95 (2.0-2.8 vsyncs) before any real present wait, versus 7-17 ms for pointer; so on a real 60 Hz display a wheel-driven zoom should be modelled as ~27 ms input->tick + present floor, i.e. ~60 ms p50 if the floor is 2 vsyncs or ~45 ms if it is 1, not 40/50. The 'we add nothing of our own' contract held on the CPU side: the REF CSS-transform page and the WebGL-in-rAF page differed by 3 ms p50 for wheel (33.1 vs 36.1 ms) and the GL-in-rAF pointer path cost one extra frame over REF (16.7 vs 7.0 ms) because REF applies the transform without waiting for rAF. Numbers were taken under load 7-13 on 4 cores; the 16 ms rAF-alignment is structural and reproduced in both runs, the p95s are not trustworthy.

sources.finding: Every API fact is confirmed in Apple's documentation JSON: CAMetalDisplayLink.preferredFrameLatency 'The only acceptable values are 1.0 and 2.0' (iOS 17+); CAMetalLayer.maximumDrawableCount 'You can set this value to 2 or 3 only ... The default value is 3' (iOS 11.2+); displaySyncEnabled is listed only for macOS 10.13+ and Mac Catalyst 13.1+ (no iOS, so no tearing mode); Android's frame-pacing doc confirms the queue 'introduces an extra frame of latency'. The input term of the model is wrong, however: Apple states 'UIKit usually delivers touches to your app at around 60 Hz, but some devices are capable of recording touch information at up to 240 Hz', so delivery adds 0–16.7 ms (mean ≈8), not the 0–1 interval (0–8.3 ms) the model assumes, and WALT's measured physical-tap→ACTION_DOWN medians on a 60 Hz Android (19.5–26.3 ms) are already 2–3 intervals at 120 Hz. Re-derived iPad: floor 2 intervals (16.7 ms) stands by API design, but typical = ≈8 ms input + 8.3 ms encode/GPU + 8.3–16.7 ms present/scan-out = 25–33 ms (3–4 intervals), 41 ms worst case; the only public end-to-end measurements of Apple's own apps on a 120 Hz iPad Pro (secondary: Dan Luu Pencil 30 ms; AnandTech Notes ≈38 ms, Procreate ≈49 ms; Apple's own marketing claim 20 ms) sit at 3.6–5.9 intervals. The N-iPad warm row should therefore read ≈33/42 ms (not 25/33); N-And 40/55 is consistent with 3–4 intervals plus a ~60 Hz-batched input term. The web→native gain on iPad shrinks from ≈20 ms to ≈12 ms (≈1.5 of the quoted 8.3 ms JND) unless the native shell also halves the input term, which Apple's docs do not promise (whether UIKit delivers at 120 Hz on ProMotion panels is not documented; the 'around 60 Hz' text dates from iOS 9).

arithmetic.finding: The arithmetic is exact: doubling in 300 ms = 3.33 levels/s; log2(1/0.7) = 0.515 levels; 0.515/3.33 = 154 ms; 1/0.7 = 1.43×; 1.2×/notch = 0.263 levels so two notches = 0.526 levels, just past the crossing; 21,416/1,246 = 17.2 events per review; log2(5) = 2.32 levels; 66.4 + 33.6 = 100; Kayser 1 − 0.259 = 74.1 % waste. The hidden assumption is that 155 ms is a point value: if gestures start at a log-uniform s in [0.5, 1) (median 2^-0.5 = 0.707, which is exactly why 0.7 is 'typical'), the lead at 3.33 levels/s is uniform on 0-300 ms with p25 = 75 ms, so the plan's 'cold level lands inside the lead at p50' pairs the p50 network with the p50 lead and the joint probability is lower (e.g. W-LAN 85 ms fill beats the lead only 72 % of the time). The sensitivity grid spans 12-500 ms (s 0.5-0.95 × 2-6 levels/s); a physical bound suggests the 3.33 levels/s pinch rate is slow for phones (fingers separating 3→6 cm at 20-30 cm/s take 100-150 ms, i.e. 6.7-10 levels/s), making a 50-90 ms median lead plausible on W-4G. The 196 ms figure is the minimum inter-burst gap over 21,416 events, so using it as a lead is conservative, but it only helps if the next burst's destination is predictable. The Brunyé percentages and counts are internally consistent but could not be checked against the paper in this lens; the pinch-rate gap is correctly flagged [unverified] and Stage-1 logging is the right dependency.

arithmetic.finding: The RGBA8 correction is right and the old '64 tiles, 1-2 MB' is refuted: a square slide whose first level ≤4096 px is exactly 4096 (e.g. 131,072 px) has 64+16+4+1 = 85 tiles = 85 MiB (66 % of 128 MiB); the canonical 100k slide has 49+16+4+1 = 70 tiles (55 %); the ≤2048 set is 21-22 tiles + thumbnail ≈ 23 MiB in both cases; '1-2 MB' for 64-85 tiles implies 16-31 KB per tile, i.e. ~80 % glass. Two refinements. First, '70-85 tiles' is only the upper half of the range: tile count depends on where the slide dimension falls between powers of two, so an 80k or 65.5k square slide gives 25+9+4+1 = 39 tiles, and non-square slides shrink the set further (100k × 50k → 39; 120k × 40k → 35) — the claim's worry that a 2:1 slide inflates the ≤2048 set is backwards (11 tiles, not 32) under the usual max-side criterion. Second, the Base Bundle '2-5 MB' encodes an unstated glass fraction: low pyramid levels contain tissue at higher density per tile and compress worse, not better — the synthetic q85 4:4:4 pyramid in tmp-tiles/ averages 96 KB/tile at its 4096-wide level and 117 KB/tile at the 2048 level (65 tiles, 6.36 MB total), and the measured IHC tile is 87-109 KB at q85-q90 4:4:4. With ~95 KB per tissue tile and ~6 KB per glass tile, 70-85 tiles come to 2.3-3.5 MB at 30-40 % tissue, 4.2-5.0 MB at 60 %, and 6.7-8.1 MB for tissue-dense slides (large resections, TMAs), i.e. 0.7-1.6 s versus 2.1-2.6 s at 25 Mbps. So 2-5 MB is a typical-biopsy figure and the slide-open prefetch should be budgeted at ≤8 MB worst case.

Two 64-layer arrays = 128 MiB is arithmetically 'exactly two' but leaves zero headroom inside a 128 MiB L0 for anything else the GPU holds (three 1170×2532 RGBA8 backbuffers alone are ≈34 MiB, plus LUTs and overlay layers), so L0 must be defined as tile slots only and the kill-threshold budget in risk 2 must add those outside it. Slot closure holds with modest margin: at DPR 3 the phone viewport is E[(1170/512+1)(2532/512+1)] = 19.5 tiles per level, a 1-tile ring adds 22.5, so two levels + ring on one level + 9-tile window + 23-tile base = 94 slots (the plan's ≈91), or 116 of 128 (91 %) if the ring is kept on both resident levels; at DPR 2 it is 71-89 slots. The 16-bit fluorescence consequence is right: r16uint 512² = 512 KiB, ×8 channels = 4 MiB per tile position, a 4× slot collapse. arithmetic.finding: The tile counts reproduce (390x844 CSS at DPR 2 = 780x1688 -> (780/512+1)(1688/512+1) = 10.8 tiles per level; DPR 3 -> 19.5), but the stated composition is wrong in two offsetting ways. 'Two levels = 22 tiles' counts the parent level at the L* count, whereas the parent covers the viewport with 4.7 tiles (DPR 2) / 7.4 (DPR 3); and the 'ring +60-90 %' is a 4K-viewport figure (+71 % at 3840x2160): a full 1-tile ring on a phone viewport adds 17.6 tiles = +163 % of L* at DPR 2 and 22.5 tiles = +115 % at DPR 3. Re-summed honestly (L* + parent + full ring + 9-tile L*+1 window + 23-tile Pinned Base) the working set is 65 MiB at DPR 2 (claim 64) and 81 MiB at DPR 3 (claim 91), so the totals hold by cancellation, not by construction. The real gap is allocation granularity: L0 is defined as <=64-layer 512^2 arrays, and both 65 and 81 tiles need two arrays, i.e. 128 MiB allocated at either DPR, leaving zero headroom for revisit caching, in-flight uploads or the moving->settled duplicate tiles held during the <=100 ms cross-fade (+11-20 MiB transient); the DPR-2 cap only pays off if arrays are sized to the budget (e.g. 32 layers). Outside L0 but in the same GPU process sit the canvas backbuffers (5.0 MiB at DPR 2 / 11.3 MiB at DPR 3, x2-3 for swap chain and compositor copy = 10-34 MiB, plus depth/stencil if not disabled). One internal inconsistency: W-iPad L0 256 MiB + L1 <=25 % (64 MiB) = 320 MiB already exceeds the G6 gate 'WebContent RSS <= 300 MB' (286 MiB) before any wasm heap or JS, so G6 must name the process it measures (textures live in the GPU process on current iOS) or the W-iPad L0 must drop. The ceiling comparisons (128 MiB vs 1.25-2 GB jetsam; 128+32+heap ~ 200-250 MB vs 224-384 MB canvas budgets) are arithmetic-consistent but unmeasured, as the claim says.

sources.finding: The individual numbers trace to real sources, but several are mischaracterised and one gate measures the wrong process. (1) WebKit on iOS runs WebGL in the GPU Process by default: PlatformEnableCocoa.h sets ENABLE_GPU_PROCESS_WEBGL_BY_DEFAULT 1 for PLATFORM(IOS_FAMILY) || PLATFORM(MAC), and UnifiedWebPreferences.yaml makes UseGPUProcessForWebGLEnabled default true under that macro, so the 128–256 MiB L0 texture budget is not in WebContent's footprint and the G6 'WebContent RSS ≤300 MB' gate cannot see it; G6/M2 must measure the GPU Process (or total) footprint. (2) The canvas budgets are not a live constraint: forum 112218 reports 224 MB on iOS 12, bug 190280 reports 256 MB (iPad) / 288 MB (iPhone X) on iOS 12, and the June-2023 commit for bug 195325 removed the canvas memory limit entirely; I could not source the '384 MB (iOS 15)' figure. (3) The '≈1.25 GB jetsam on iPad Air 3' (forum 668999, Dec 2020) is the termination point of a WebGL canvas-resize memory leak on iOS 14.2 that the poster says was fixed in iOS 14.3 — a leak kill, not a budget measurement. (4) The 2048 MB ActiveHard figure (forum 823061, Apr 2026) is a kernel log line for com.apple.WebKit.WebContent on iPhone 17 Pro, iOS 26.3–26.4.1, under 'heavy CSS animations' with no WebGL; an Apple Frameworks Engineer replied 'iPhones do indeed have stricter jetsam limits than iPads'; corroborating points: InactiveSoft 1536 MB on an iPhone SE (bug 264370) and ~1.5 GB usable on iPhone 12 Pro iOS 17.5.1 / ~3 GB on 15 Pro (bug 277848, RESOLVED INVALID). Bug 312727 is a jetsam while scrolling long articles, not WebGL texture use; 253172 was a 2023 pan/zoom jetsam regression duplicated to 252237. (5) Ruffle's wgpu-oom label has 900 open and 110 closed issues today — 1,010 is the total, not the open count. (6) Arithmetic: 390×844 CSS gives 10.85 tiles/level at DPR 2 and 19.53 at DPR 3; two levels × ring 1.6–1.9 + 9 + 23 = 66.7–73.2 MiB at DPR 2 (60.2–63.4 MiB if the ring applies to the current level only) and 94.5–106.2 MiB at DPR 3 (82.8–88.6 MiB ring-on-one-level), so '≈64 / ≈91 MiB' is the optimistic edge at DPR 2 and mid-range at DPR 3; both still close inside 128 MiB, with ≤45 MiB headroom at DPR 3 before the 32 MiB CPU-side L1 is counted.

Two consequences the plan's prose glosses over follow from the same numbers. First, the budget binds only when tiles arrive faster than 2-4 per frame = 120-240 tiles/s, which at 80-109 KB per tile is 77-210 Mbit/s: never on 4G (0.5-1 tile/frame at 25 Mbit/s, so 'hidden under transfer' is correct), marginally on 100 Mbit/s broadband (1.9-2.6 tiles/frame), and always from L1/L2 or LAN. So a 20-tile revisit or zoom-out served from the decoded CPU cache costs 83-167 ms of upload on a phone, which contradicts the section 4.4 promise that 'zoom-out and revisits [are] instant' at the 2 MiB/frame end (167 ms > 100 ms). Second, the G5 pass criterion (<=2 ms per 512^2 upload) times the 4 MiB/frame budget is 8 ms of main-thread upload per frame, 48 % of a 16.7 ms frame, so the 4 MiB budget is only safe if per-tile cost is <=1 ms or uploads leave the main thread; the separate 'no single stall >8 ms' tolerance is 4x the pass criterion. The absolute per-tile costs on iOS Safari and Mali-G52 are unmeasured, exactly as the claim states.

arithmetic.finding: The size figures are byte-exact: 3,143,639 B raw and 1,028,041 B gzip -9 for the dual-backend module (0.980 MiB = 1.028 MB), 2,782,954 / 934,936 B for WebGL2-only, 934,753 / 223,390 B for WebGPU-only; every 'MB' in the corpus is a MiB, and '+0.68 MB gz' is WebGL-only minus WebGPU-only (711,546 B = 0.679 MiB), whereas dual minus WebGPU-only is 804,651 B (0.767 MiB), so recommended.md section 2 understates what dropping wgpu's WebGL2 backend saves and the G1 '<=1.0 MB gz' gate is ambiguous at exactly this boundary (passes in MiB by 2 %, fails in MB by 2.8 %). The compile-time sub-claim is refuted by a factor of 5-10: the 5-8 ms figure was taken with V8's default --wasm-lazy-compilation (true in V8 12.4), which validates and defers code generation (3.14 MB in 5.2 ms would be 605 MB/s). With --no-wasm-lazy-compilation the same x86 takes 36-65 ms on 4 threads and 87-118 ms single-threaded (32-36 MB/s Liftoff throughput, unchanged with --liftoff --no-wasm-tier-up). Lazy mode does not remove that cost; it moves it into the first calls, i.e. into G2's 'first frame' for whatever fraction of the module executes then (for a wgpu WebGL backend that includes naga's runtime WGSL->GLSL translation). What can be checked is whether the numbers are mutually consistent and whether the design consequences drawn from them close arithmetically, and they do: the same values (OPFS Chrome 102 / Firefox 111 / Safari 15.2; 60 % / 15 % / min(10 % disk, 10 GiB); SW 50 / 250 / >500 ms; 7-day ITP deletion) appear identically in 05 F7, A-web-core §2, gap-3 row 8 and recommended §9 with no drift. The 'SW off the hot path' consequence is arithmetically forced: a 250 ms mobile cold start equals 100 % of the W-4G TTS p50 gate (250 ms) and 250 % of the W-iPad gate (100 ms); a 50 ms desktop cold start equals 100 % of the W-LAN gate (50 ms). Quota is never the binding constraint for the L2 design: the 300-500 MB phone L2 budget is 6-10 % of even the 15 % WKWebView share of a 32 GB device (4.8 GB) and ~1 % of a 60 % share of 64 GB (38 GB), so only the 7-day deletion matters, which is what the plan says. One caution the claim understates: gap-3 itself grades the persist()-does-not-help inference 'Med' (absence of an isPersisted check on the ITP path, not a positive statement), and open question 10 leaves the exact ITP trigger semantics for third-party-embedded origins unverified, so 'refillable L2, never store of record' is the right design regardless of how that resolves.

empirical.finding: The storage facts hold where they can be checked, but two numbers need restating. Chromium's enforced per-origin quota is indeed 60% of the disk (quota_features.cc PoolSizeRatio 0.8 x quota_settings.h kDefaultPerStorageKeyRatio 0.75), yet the value an app can read is privacy-capped: quota_manager_impl.cc CalculateReportedQuota returns usage + 10 GiB whenever the disk is >= 10 GiB, and headless Chromium 153 on a 270 GB disk reported navigator.storage.estimate().quota = 10,737,418,240 B (4.0% of disk) in a persistent profile and 3.26 GB in an ephemeral context (incognito pool = 15-20% of RAM, /3 per origin); persist() returned false in both. So any L2 sizing logic must not read estimate() as '60% of disk'. The Service Worker cold-start figure is overstated for current Chromium: with the SW stopped via CDP ServiceWorker.stopAllWorkers (stopped->starting->running confirmed in events), a fetch answered by a 3-line SW took median 11.9 ms (9 runs, 8.7-37.9 ms) versus 2.7 ms warm, i.e. about 9 ms cold-start overhead on a contended x86 box, not 50 ms; the 50/250/500 ms figures come from a 2017 web.dev post and real SWs (routing, Workbox) are larger, so a 2024+ phone is plausibly 30-60 ms, which keeps 'SW off the hot path' defensible but weakens 'SW never'. OPFS FileSystemSyncAccessHandle exists in Chromium 153 and BCD gives Chrome 102 / Chrome Android 109 / Firefox 111 / Safari 15.2 (claim omits the Android 109 date); kept-open sync-handle random 60 KB reads cost p50 <=0.2 ms, p99 <=0.5 ms, while open+read+close per tile file costs p50 1.0-1.2 ms, p99 3-4 ms and writing one file per tile 2-3 ms vs 0.1-1.1 ms into one shard file, which argues for a shard-file L2 with kept-open handles. WebKit's monitoredDataTypes() (prior download of WebResourceLoadStatisticsStore.cpp) does list DOMCache and FileSystem and isPersisted is consulted only in NetworkStorageManager eviction paths, consistent with the claim; Safari/WKWebView (15%) and Firefox (min 10%, 10 GiB) could not be observed here and rest on MDN text.

arithmetic.finding: The arithmetic that this claim underwrites closes against the raw bench JSONs, not just the note's table. Per-tile rows sum exactly (decode + copy-out + messaging = round trip to 0.001 ms: 2.926 / 2.907 / 3.164 ms for 1 / 2 / 3 workers), and the no-SAB overhead (copy-out + messaging) is 0.41 / 0.54 / 0.58 ms, i.e. 16-23 % of a 2.4-2.6 ms x86 wasm decode, so '≈0.5 ms per tile' is a fair midpoint. The 20-tile burst gives 53.81 / 24.57 = 2.19x on 3 workers (73 % of the 3x ideal; the relevant ideal is 3x, not 4x, since the main thread is excluded by design), 1.66x on 2, and 0.94x on 1, so clamp(hardwareConcurrency − 1, 1, 3) yields no throughput gain at all on a hardwareConcurrency = 2 device, only main-thread offload, exactly the failure mode the load-bearing note names. Projecting to an A55 at the corpus's own 3-5x factor (7.5-12.5 ms/tile) gives 68-114 ms wall for 20 tiles on 3 workers, consistent with (slightly better than) recommended §4.4's 100-150 ms W-4G decode row, so the row is conservative rather than optimistic. Caveats that bound the confidence: the measurement is Node worker_threads on a 4-vCPU x86 Xeon with zune-jpeg wasm, not libjpeg-turbo wasm in a browser on big.LITTLE silicon, and the inline baseline is an idle serial loop, so the 2.2x is a throughput shape, not a device number. The primary-source parts (atomics Unstable at 1.99.1, BCD webview_android false, relaxed-SIMD Safari preview-only, the Ruffle/rerun/egui/Bevy/Graphite/Aladin survey, !Send + !Sync) are not testable by this lens.

On a plain origin typeof SharedArrayBuffer is 'undefined' and crossOriginIsolated is false; WebAssembly.Memory({shared:true}) can still be constructed, but posting its buffer (or the Memory object) to a Worker throws DataCloneError 'SharedArrayBuffer transfer requires self.crossOriginIsolated', so there is no cross-thread shared memory without COOP+COEP; with the two headers SAB is a function and coi is true. The gap-2 decision table recomputes exactly: weights sum to 19 (max 95) and A = 72, B = 78, C = 82 from the printed cell scores, so the '82 vs 78' ranking is not a transcription error. The release cadence v27 2025-10 → v28 2025-12 → v29 2026-03 → v30 2026-07 is 2 / 3 / 4 months, mean 3.0, so 'roughly quarterly' holds and the corpus's '28→30 in eight months' is 7 months by month arithmetic (inclusive counting explains the 8). Testing the sentence 'every first-byte row assumes edge server time 2/8 ms' against recommended §4.3's own RTT classes exposes an inconsistency: W-LAN (RTT <1/3 + 2/8 = 3/11 vs quoted 4/12) and W-4G (45/200 + 2/8 = 47/208 vs quoted 57/226, i.e. conservative) close, but W-BB and W-iPad quote a first-byte p50 of 19 ms against an RTT p50 of 25 ms, which is physically impossible on a warm connection (first byte ≥ one RTT); 19 ms is 02-F9's model built on Ookla's 9 ms median fixed latency, so either §4.3's 'CDN edge 25/50 ms' class is mislabeled (should be ≈9-15/50) or the first-byte row should read ≥27/58 ms. The p95 column (50 + 8 = 58) closes either way, and the cold-fill totals move by <5 %. A second hidden assumption: a per-tile p50 first byte governs a 20-tile fill only because the plan coalesces the centre tiles into one bundle; with per-tile GETs the fill is bounded by the slowest of 20, i.e. the per-tile ≈p95 (58 / 226 ms), which 02-F9 itself notes. Little's law on Iris (5,000 req/s x 21 ms = 105 in flight; 8 cores / 5,000 req/s = 1.6 ms CPU per request if saturated; latency/service ≈ 13x) shows the 21 ms is a loaded-latency figure and the unloaded service time is ≈1-2 ms, which supports 'p99 ≤ 10 ms hot service time' as lenient for RAM hits (a 15-tile 0.9 MB bundle is ≈0.2 ms of memcpy) but means the gate is meaningful only with a stated load, since at S = 1.6 ms an M/M/1 queue keeps p99 latency under 10 ms only below ≈26 % utilisation. The arithmetic built on them mostly closes: browser floor = input 4-16 + ≈2 vsyncs 33 + draw ≤4 = 37-53 ms, matching '≈35-55 ms' and placing the web floor at 3.4-4.8x the 11 ms direct-drag JND; the 155 ms pinch lead recomputes to 154 ms (log2(1/0.7) levels at 3.33 levels/s); Brunyé's '66.4 % ≥5x' is the same statement as '66 % ≥2.3 levels' (log2 5 = 2.32) and '34 % short bursts' is its complement (33.6 %). The statement that 120 Hz buys 'exactly the smallest perceivable improvement' is wrong arithmetic, however: one 120 Hz interval is 8.33 ms, but a pipeline of N vsyncs saves N x 8.33 ms when the rate doubles, so a 2-vsync floor saves 16.7 ms and a 3-vsync floor 25 ms, and the corpus's own iPad tables show the native 120 Hz shell cutting warm I2P from 45 to 25 ms (20 ms). The 8.3 ms = 8.3 ms coincidence should not be used as an argument; the real saving is 2-3x the JND, which strengthens the 120 Hz case rather than weakening it (the claim's own test plan flags this). arithmetic.finding: The frame-budget arithmetic in the claim is right: 16.7 − (6-12) leaves 4.7-10.7 ms, 6-12 ms is 36-72 % of a 60 Hz frame, and 0.5-2 ms is 3-12 % at 60 Hz and 6-24 % at 120 Hz. The two OSD overhead figures are reconcilable only if 0.5-2 ms is read as a desktop estimate (C §3.3 states it for the 44-tile x 3-level 4K desktop configuration); scaled by the corpus's own 3-5x A55 factor it is 1.5-10 ms on the W-4G floor (9-60 % of the frame), which is why C's §3.4 table shows 2-4 ms for the post-R2 Android row. The sharper inconsistency is inside proposal C itself: its R2 replacement trigger is '_updateLevelsForViewport > 2 ms/frame with 44 tiles x 3 levels on the floor Android', yet its own MVP model puts that quantity at 6-12 ms on Android, so by C's numbers the trigger fires at M0, not in months 8-11, which undercuts the 'replace only when a named metric fails' sequencing. The default-settings facts I could check from the locally cached tiledimage.js (dl/tiledimage.js) hold: _currentMaxTilesPerFrame starts at maxTilesPerFrame x 10 on each fully-loaded→incomplete transition and decays by ceil-halving per frame to a single shared candidate list across all levels, giving a dispatch schedule of 10, 5, 3, 2, 1, 1, ... tiles per frame; a 20-tile phone viewport is fully requested after 4 frames (67 ms at 60 Hz) but a 44-tile desktop viewport needs 28 frames (467 ms) and a 54-tile 2x-DPR viewport 38 frames (633 ms), whereas maxTilesPerFrame 100 dispatches all in one frame. Any 'X-times faster than OpenSeadragon' claim against default settings would therefore be measuring this request-rationing artefact plus the 1.2 s / stiffness-6.5 spring (50 % settled at 128 ms, 90 % at 425 ms, 99 % at 850 ms), not rendering; the tuned profile must be the comparator and OSD's per-frame CPU must be reported separately. The npm date, #2906 status and the drawer internals (per-tile texImage2D, no generateMipmap, drawImage composite) are primary-source items outside this lens.

empirical.finding: The source facts are all verified in the npm 6.1.1 build: DEFAULT_SETTINGS maxTilesPerFrame 1, imageLoaderLimit 0, immediateRender false, blendTime 0, placeholderFillStyle null, animationTime 1.2, springStiffness 6.5, minScrollDeltaTime 50; _currentMaxTilesPerFrame starts at 10x and is halved each frame; the WebGL drawer uploads each tile with gl.texImage2D, sets TEXTURE_MIN_FILTER to LINEAR/NEAREST with no generateMipmap anywhere in the file, and composites the rendering canvas into the output canvas with 2D drawImage; the scheduler lives in private TiledImage._updateLevelsForViewport/_updateLevel. The measured per-frame costs resolve the perf judge's inconsistency as two different states rather than a contradiction. Running OSD 6.1.1 in headless Chromium 153 against the stage-0 16384x12288 pyramid over loopback at 1920x1080 with World.update/World.draw timed at 5 us resolution (COOP+COEP), the settled state with all 24 visible tiles resident costs World.update 0.005 ms and World.draw 0.33 ms (canvas) / 0.5 ms (WebGL) per forced frame, a whole updateOnce of 0.4-0.6 ms, so the '0.5-2 ms/frame end-state' estimate is correct and even generous (it would be ~2-3 ms with a 5x A55 factor and twice the tiles). During the 8x spring zoom and the pan, however, the scheduler alone costs 0.42-0.59 ms p50 and 4-5 ms p99 per frame on x86 (22-31 tiles over 2 levels, 60 fps, 0 frames over 16.7 ms with the canvas drawer), and under Chrome's 4x CPU throttle 3.4 ms p50 and 32 ms p99 with 26 of 39 zoom frames over 16.7 ms and 11 long tasks (WebGL draw inflated by SwiftShader texture uploads), so '6-12 ms/frame of OSD scheduler time on floor Android' is a p90-class cost of animating frames on a slow phone, not a steady or end-state figure. Two side observations matter for the stopgap and comparator roles: with the WebGL drawer the frame rate collapsed to 2.7-7 fps during tile uploads (software GL) and OSD's per-frame tile rationing then stretched the 8x-zoom fill to 5.8-6.5 s versus 1.22 s (= animationTime) with the canvas drawer, showing that maxTilesPerFrame couples fill rate to frame rate; and the 44 tiles x 3 levels case was not reachable at 1080p (24 tiles settled, 31-48 in transitions), so any 'X times faster than OpenSeadragon' claim must report OSD's own update and draw times per state. All runs had a sibling agent's load average of 7.6-9.4 on 4 cores, so x86 numbers are upper bounds; a Mali/A55 device test is still needed.
